How much more can SA take?

By: Floris Kotze | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A country in turmoil, from corruption to public sector strikes, when will this end?

Unique Selling Point:
We look at the health sector strike, what did it really cost South Africa? With another shutdown planned for the week ahead, how much more can SA take?

Summary:
We speak to Dr Percy Mahlati, Deputy Director General for Hospital Services, National Health Department. Was 3% worth the lives that we lost? Why is government not listening?
Journalist Mark Heywood also shares his opinion of where the country should be heading.

Further information:
It is a news insert that starts with us looking back athe last few months, the public sector strikes of the past week concludes with the question, how much more can we take?

Script:


Montage of strikes, chaos…
SABC AUDIO
Preventing healthcare workers and also patience and getting medication…
Nehawu has embarked on a nationwide strike…
Major focus has been on disrupting health services…
Link
The past couple of months have been quite rough with rolling blackouts, corruption and political instability but it doesn't end there….
VO:
On the 6th of March NEHAWU members went on a Public Service strike. The health sector was hardest hit. 6 people died.

Mark:
When the NEHAWU strike turned violent, it’s part of a of a toxic broth that is simmering in our country and that is looking for an outlet and the strike gave it an outlet.
VO: Mark Heywood is a South African human rights and social justice activist. He feels there is no justification for violence.
NEHAWU could also targeted its demonstrations and it's only got other sources could have targeted at the office is a provincial health departments could have targeted at the national health department but to deliberately impede services and cause that type of disruption I feel was was immoral as well as unlawful
Dr Percy:
It has put the risk of those who already have their lives compromised by illness and disease while services are being withheld from them.
VO: Dr Percy Mahlati is Deputy Director General in the department of health… responsible for Hospital Services nationally.
Dr Percy:
The major focus has been in hospital that are serving disadvantaged Communities, we just do not understand what went into the planning and thinking and all that of those who orchestrated the strike
Mark:
The strain on our nurses and doctors has been growing. We have a huge human resource shortage and yet what we're talking about is a constitutionally enshrined right the right of everyone to have access to health care services. The budget for the Healthcare system has been declining for a decade.


Dr Percy:
You can’t have a shrinking tax base and then think that you'll be able to provide for every demand in society. Therefore we've got to look at how do we grow our economy and I can assure you even if government gave that 10% now, next year they'll be demanding 20% and go on strike.
Mac:
Do you know how many lives have been lost?
Dr Percy:
So far the reported lies that led to the strike at 6 however it is highly possible that is not only 6, it could be more than those.
VO:
CARTE BLANCHE requested an interview with NEHAWU, but they declined.
Mark:
The nastiness and violence that we saw in the Healthcare workers strike should be taken as a warning of a nastiness and a violence and a lack of respect for the rule of law that could take place on a far larger scale should the poor of this country decide that actually we have no stake in the system and the way that it's running at the moment and we getting close to that point.
LINK:
It's undeniable that South Africans have had enough with all the broken promises people are now choosing to go to the streets and of the looming EFF’s looming national shutdown small can we take?
Mark:
I haven't given up hope the strike also showed us another side that there were many nurses many doctors who continue to go to work despite the threats of the violence and the intimidation, and I still think that that is the heart of our country, you know, that's what gave us 1994 that's what helps us to avoid a civil war. We have the resources. I think that we have the people and we still have the Vision. We just have to find a way to put those three things together effectively.

11 Seconder
Many lives were lost during the health sector strike why did this happen and who was responsible?
